summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on grounds that include sex, gender and sexual orientation. The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act of 2000 gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court, which hears complaints of unfair discrimination, hate speech and harassment on grounds including gender identity. The Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act, signed into law in May 2024, places sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics inside a statutory hate-crime and hate-speech regime; its hate-speech offence requires a clear intention to be harmful, to incite harm or to promote hatred.

Nothing in South African law criminalises gender identity or consensual adult sexual conduct. The common-law offences of sodomy and unnatural sexual act were struck down by the Constitutional Court in 1998 and applied retroactively to 27 April 1994.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court sitting as an Equality Court, in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Case 2024/070075), held that refusing a transgender inmate the gender-affirming health care prescribed for her falls below the required standard of health care, and that refusing her feminising clothing and accessories is likewise unlawful. The orders compel the Department of Correctional Services to provide prescribed hormone treatment at state expense, to permit clothing and cosmetics expressing her gender identity, to implement the accommodations she requires and to enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The South African Human Rights Commission welcomed the ruling the same day as an affirmation of the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities.

Detention therefore carries a documented, now enforceable floor rather than an assumed one. Reporting in August 2025 recorded that the Department of Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners, while rights organisations doubted that it was being implemented in practice; the November 2025 orders direct enforcement of that procedure.

Legal gender recognition runs through the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act, in force since 2003, which allows a person to change sex status in the population registry and obtain identity documents and passports carrying their gender identity. Surgery is not required, but medical or surgical treatment such as hormone replacement therapy is, a requirement that rights organisations describe as pathologising identity and that locks people out of recognition; reform toward self-determination was still pending as of March 2026. The binary classification also excludes non-binary people entirely. The cost of affirming one's gender is described as dauntingly high, and mismatched documents expose trans people to humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 report by Gender Dynamix documents a trans woman refused help in filing a domestic-violence case after showing her identity document, amid police mockery.

In October 2021 the Department of Home Affairs announced plans to introduce gender-neutral identification on South African identity cards, which would make the country the first African state to do so, with an identity-management document estimating 530,000 non-binary residents. The head of policy confirmed the changes would take a few years as they move through consultation to legislation.

Facility access remains contested. A 2024 academic analysis asks whether excluding transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms constitutes unfair discrimination under the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act read with section 9 of the Constitution, and concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in access to facilities.

Violence against visible trans women is documented. Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a Tshwane tavern on 26 December 2024 that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; an arrest was reported the following month. A country overview updated in March 2026 finds that violence disproportionately affects black lesbian, transgender and gender-nonconforming people in township communities.

Gender-affirming care is available but unevenly. Hormone replacement therapy can be accessed from age 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent. Private care is concentrated in the main urban centres while public systems face long waits, which pushes rural patients to travel to major cities. In December 2024 activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year.

Partner recognition is established. The Civil Union Act of 2006 provides for same-sex marriage, and court decisions before and after it extended immigration benefits, employment and pension benefits and joint adoption to same-sex couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex falls within the class those decisions protect.
tangentialFactors:
The 2024 hate-crime statute drew sustained criticism before and after assent. Human Rights Watch and other legal experts warned that its wording is vague, threatens freedom of expression, and has been likened to the Suppression of Communism Act, 1950; the hate-speech provision was tightened after 2016 public consultation to require a clear intention to harm.

State machinery addressing LGBTI violence predates the statute. The Department of Justice established a National Task Team in 2011 and a National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities in April 2014, covering sex- and gender-based violence with a rapid response team for unsolved cases; earlier, Justice Minister Jeff Radebe launched a programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence citing the Constitution's equality clause.

Public opinion is comparatively favourable but not uniform. A 2017 ILGA poll found 67% backing equal rights for gay and lesbian people and 72% for transgender people, while 24% still said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals against 57% who disagreed. An Ipsos poll in May 2021 found 71% supporting some legal recognition for same-sex couples. South Africa ranks among the strongest performers in the 2025 Spartacus Gay Travel Index and the Equaldex LGBT Equality Index.

Enforcement of protection is contested. Activists have accused police of negligent handling of killings, including nine allegedly related murders of gay men between 2010 and 2013, and ActionAid has condemned impunity; lesbians have been murdered, beaten and subjected to so-called corrective rape, including among pupils. In 2012 Contralesa petitioned to remove LGBT rights from the Constitution and the ANC parliamentary caucus rejected the request.
localsOnly:
Conversion therapy is not prohibited under the Children's Act 38 of 2005. A bill introduced in 2021 would ban it on children; it followed the deaths of three teenagers aged 15 to 19 at a conversion therapy camp whose owners were convicted of murder and child abuse in February 2015.

Transgender minors can access hormone therapy from 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent. Private provision is mostly urban and public systems face long waits, so rural young people must travel to major cities for care. A non-binary teenager, Zade de Kock, petitioned the Department of Home Affairs over being compelled to use inaccurate gender markers throughout his schooling.

Residents seeking legal gender recognition must satisfy the medical requirements of the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act, and the binary registry structure offers no route for non-binary people; advocacy toward a self-determination model remained unresolved as of March 2026.

Reporting domestic violence while carrying an identity document that does not match presentation can end the encounter before it begins. The Gender Dynamix 2024 account of a trans woman turned away from filing a case, with police mockery, indicates the risk sits at the point of reporting rather than only in the underlying offence.
outOfScopeNotes:
No provisions on border checks, entry screening or security screening of travellers are sourced for this jurisdiction. The only screening-type policy described in the inventory concerns blood donation: the six-month deferral for men who have sex with men applied until 2014 and was replaced by a gender-neutral rule covering any donor with a new sexual partner in the previous six months or more than one partner.

Whether exclusion from gender-segregated facilities constitutes unfair discrimination is unresolved. The inventory contains academic argument on the point and no court ruling, statute or regulator decision settling it.

The gender-neutral identity card announced in October 2021 is unresolved as to enactment. The inventory records announcement, an estimate of 530,000 non-binary residents and a policy statement that the change would take a few years through consultation to legislation, but no passed law.

The status of the 2021 conversion-therapy bill is unresolved. Its introduction is sourced; passage or rejection is not.

No trans-specific violence rate with a denominator is sourced. The only quantitative figure available is a raw count of five LGBTQIA+ murders reported by a national NGO for December 2024, a monthly figure covering the whole acronym with no population or time-normalised base, so it carries no magnitude and supports no comparison.

Nationwide implementation of the Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure for transgender inmates is unresolved. Its existence is sourced, rights organisations questioned implementation in August 2025, and the November 2025 orders direct enforcement without the inventory recording whether compliance followed.

The fees and administrative costs of legal gender recognition are described qualitatively as high; no schedule of charges is sourced.
